metadata.title: Interpreting mathematics performance in PISA_ Taking account of reading performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2009 China Trial data from Fangshan District of Beijing, with a three-stage sampling design (regions → schools → 15-year-olds), and it targets academic-track students only. To address sampling error and PV-related measurement error, the authors state that PISA sampling weights and all replicate weights were employed when applicable, and they use normalized student final weights for the analyses. Plausible values for mathematics and reading are incorporated using replicate-weight procedures, consistent with PISA technical guidance. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly indicates that both final and replicate weights were used via IEA IDB Analyzer and Stata pooling of the five PV datasets.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2009 China Trial data for Fangshan District of Beijing, sampling 25 secondary academic schools (out of 52) and including 15-year-old students enrolled in the academic track. The analytic sample excludes the three students with missing ESCS values; all other variables were complete. Final sample size is 607 students across 25 schools.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 China Trial (Fangshan District, Beijing) Mathematics literacy (PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level multilevel models (MLM): M2 reading effect β=0.833 (p<0.001); M1: SCH_ESCS β=91.684 (p<0.001), male β=16.739 (p<0.05); variance explained: M1 within-school 1%, between-school 40%; M2 adds reading increases within-school explained by 51% more and between-school by 46% more (as reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 China Trial (Fangshan District, Beijing) the study leveraged overall reading performance together with gender and ESCS (student and school levels) to predict mathematics performance (PVs), finding that reading performance had a strong positive association with mathematics (βreading=0.833, p<0.001) after controlling for background factors. This indicates that interpreting PISA mathematics results without accounting for reading demands may misrepresent which students are struggling with mathematics versus reading-related comprehension processes.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2009 China Trial data from Fangshan District of Beijing (academic-track 15-year-olds; N=607 after excluding 3 students with missing ESCS) to explain mathematics performance (PVs) using reading performance and reading subareas. The authors fit two-level multilevel models with students nested in schools, incorporating PISA plausible values via the five-PV approach and pooling results using Stata’s MI procedure, while applying sampling weights and replicate weights through IEA IDB Analyzer. The key result is that overall reading performance strongly predicts mathematics performance (β=0.833, p<0.001), and the association is concentrated in specific reading aspects (Integrate & Interpret; Reflect & Evaluate) and in reading non-continuous texts (β=0.436, p<0.001). The study reports no causal identification; it is observational and therefore cannot establish that reading causes mathematics outcomes, and it uses a single local context that may limit generalizability.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train or evaluate machine learning algorithms; instead, it uses two-level multilevel modeling (MLM) with PISA plausible values and survey weights. Therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty (no ML predictive pipeline), while the substantive findings come from regression-based multilevel associations rather than ML model performance.
